original_value: AbstractRecent urban studies have used human mobility data such as taxi trajectories and smartcard data as a complementary way to identify the social functions of land use. However, little work has been conducted to reveal how multi‐modal transportation data impact on this identification process. In our study, we propose a data‐driven approach that addresses the relationships between travel behavior and urban structure: first, multi‐modal transportation data are aggregated to extract explicit statistical features; then, topic modeling methods are applied to transform these explicit statistical features into latent semantic features; and finally, a classification method is used to identify functional zones with similar latent topic distributions. Two 10‐day‐long “big” datasets from the 2,370 bicycle stations of the public bicycle‐sharing system, and up to 9,992 taxi cabs within the core urban area of Hangzhou City, China, as well as point‐of‐interest data are tested to reveal the extent to which different travel modes contribute to the detection and understanding of urban land functions. Our results show that: (1) using latent semantic features delineated from the topic modeling process as the classification input outperforms approaches using explicit statistical features; (2) combining multi‐modal data visibly improves the accuracy and consistency of the identified functional zones; and (3) the proposed data‐driven approach is also capable of identifying mixed land use in the urban space. This work presents a novel attempt to uncover the hidden linkages between urban transportation patterns with urban land use and its functions.

result.paraphrase: Recent urban studies have leveraged human mobility data, including taxi trajectories and smartcard records, as a complementary means of identifying the social functions of land use. Yet little research has examined how multi-modal transportation data affect this identification process. In our study, we introduce a data-driven approach that captures the relationship between travel behavior and urban structure: multi-modal transportation data are first aggregated to extract explicit statistical features; topic modeling is then applied to convert these into latent semantic features; and finally, a classification method identifies functional zones with similar latent topic distributions. We test two 10-day “big” datasets from 2,370 bicycle stations in a public bike-sharing system and up to 9,992 taxis in the core urban area of Hangzhou City, China, together with point-of-interest data, to assess how different travel modes contribute to detecting and understanding urban land functions. The results indicate that (1) using latent semantic features derived from topic modeling as classification input outperforms methods based on explicit statistical features; (2) combining multi-modal data noticeably improves the accuracy and consistency of the identified functional zones; and (3) the proposed data-driven approach can also identify mixed land use in urban space. This study offers a novel effort to uncover the hidden connections between urban transportation patterns, urban land use, and its functions.
